# Historical GIS: Structuring, mapping and analysing geographies of the past.

Gregory, Ian N. and Healey, Richard G. (2007) Historical GIS: Structuring, mapping and analysing geographies of the past. Progress in Human Geography, 31 (5). pp. 638-653. ISSN 0309-1325

## Abstract

The last 10 years have seen a sudden rise in interest in the use of Geographical Information Systems (GIS) in historical research. This has led to a field that has become known as `historical GIS'. This development started in the more quantitative ends of the discipline but has spread to encompass qualitative research as well. Interest in historical GIS is not restricted to researchers who would previously have regarded themselves as historical geographers, but has in fact led to an increased awareness of the importance of geography from across the discipline of history. This paper introduces historical GIS and critically evaluates how it is affecting the practice of historical geography.

## Abstract

This article discusses the most important recent contributions in the field of Indigenous health history. This scholarship implicates health and medicine in the complicated work of the long and continuing project of colonization and the building of a white settler nation in Canada. Four key terms in this work will be discussed: starvation, experimentation, segregation, and trauma. I will show how these terms, and the historians who use them, have sharpened the broader analytics of race and colonialism in Canada as they operate in the field of Indigenous health history.

# Making space for an archaeology of place

Making space for an archaeology of place

Making space for an archaeology of place

Rather than attempt to write a balanced or complete overview of the application of GIS to archaeology (which would inevitably end up being didactic and uncritical) this article sets out to present a discursive and contentious position with the deliberate aim of stimulating further debate about the future role of GIS within our discipline.
To this end, existing applications of GIS to archaeology are reviewed, concentrating on two areas of application, predictive modelling and visibility analyses, and on their wider disciplinary context. It is argued that GIS cannot be simplistically held to have been a 'good thing' or a 'bad thing' for archaeology, but rather that these different application areas may be analysed separately and found to have quite different qualities. Although they are in no sense alternatives to one another, the areas of predictive modelling and visibility analysis can be seen to represent quite different agendas for the development of an archaeology of space and/or place.
The development of correlative predictive models is considered first, both from the perspective of explanation and of cultural resource management. The arguments against predictive modelling as a means of explanation are rehearsed and it is found to be over-generalising, deterministic and de-humanised. As a consequence, it is argued that predictive modelling is now essentially detached from contemporary theoretical archaeological concerns. Moreover, it is argued to be an area with significant unresolved methodological problems and, far more seriously, that it presents very real dangers for the future representativity of archaeological records.
Second, the development of GIS-based visibility analysis is reviewed. This is also found to be methodologically problematic and incomplete. However, it is argued that visibility studies — in direct contrast to predictive modelling — have remained firmly situated within contemporary theoretical debates, notably about how human actors experience places (phenomenology) and perceive their surroundings (cognition). As such, it is argued that visibility analysis has the potential to continue to contribute positively to the wider development of archaeological thinking, notably through laying the foundations of a human-centred archaeology of space.
The paper concludes by qualifying the claim that there is a 'hidden agenda' for archaeological applications of GIS (Wheatley 1993), particularly by making it clear that this does not imply an attempt to distort the discipline. Instead, this is explained in terms of institutional and disciplinary inertia that should be addressed through greater debate and communication over these issues.

L44: #### Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia
L45:

L51: This elegantly written and insightful book provides a geographical history of the Indian reserve in British Columbia. Cole Harris analyzes the impact of reserves on Native lives and livelihoods and considers how, in light of this, the Native land question might begin to be resolved.
L52: The account begins in the early nineteenth-century British Empire and then follows Native land policy – and Native resistance to it – in British Columbia from the Douglas treaties in the early 1850s to the formal transfer of reserves to the Dominion in 1938.
L53: Making Native Space clarifies and informs the current debate on the Native land question. It presents the most comprehensive account available of perhaps the most critical mapping of space ever undertaken in BC – the drawing of the lines that separated the tiny plots of land reserved for Native people from the rest.
L54: 
L55: Geographers, historians, anthropologists, and anybody interested in and involved in the politics of treaty negotiation in British Columbia should read this book.

L74@P3: about black femininity, racial superiority, and difference are spatialized,
L75@P3: consequently curtailing subaltern geographic desires and opportunities. In
L76@P3: this case, the historical and historically present body is at stake, frequently
L77@P3: returning us to questions of geographic captivity, ownership, and dispossession as they are connected to corporeal schemas. Second, black women’s
L78@P3: unique geographic concerns are concealed by racial, sexual, and economic
L79@P3: processes. That is, the dispossessed black female body is often equated with
L80@P3: the ungeographic, and black women’s spatial knowledges are rendered

L207@P6: Sylvia Wynter is interested in sociospatial and intellectual epochs wherein
L208@P6: the category of human, and representations of humanness, come to be
L209@P6: represented as Man. She suggests the European arrival in the New World,
L210@P6: economic expansions, and new religious and secular politics ruptured
L211@P6: existing planetary organization and forced a reconsideration of how the

L214@P6: of humanness began to be organized differently. Wynter’s theoretical strategy is to trace how Man comes to represent the only viable expression of
L215@P6: humanness, in effect, overrepresenting itself discursively and empirically.

L217@P6: voyages to the New World. These moments correspond with the conceptualization of the encountered and encountering human (Man1), who has
L218@P6: traveled (materially and imaginatively) to the New World for socioreligious exploratory purposes; and the imperialist political human (Man2),

L220@P6: Both of these inventions are struggling to develop a cohesive human subject that can consistently correspond with changing intellectual fields.

L1@P0: The Imperial Background
L2@P0: When the proprietary colony of Vancouver Island was created in 1849 and
L3@P0: the Crown colony of British Columbia in 1858, the zenith of the British
L4@P0: empire still lay ahead and a long history of British imperialism and colonialism lay behind. The modern history of the latter is usually considered to
L5@P0: have begun in Scotland and Ireland, but well before the end of the seventeenth century the relevance of overseas colonies to the prosperity of the
L6@P0: mother country was widely accepted in England.1
L7@P0:  Over the years thereafter,
L8@P0: economic motives, calculations of geopolitical advantage and of imperial
L9@P0: grandeur, concern for the plight of the British poor, the opportunity to
L10@P0: spread Protestant Christianity, and a sense of responsibility to civilize savage
L11@P0: peoples had all justified, in various permutations and combinations, the British
L12@P0: government’s involvement in the colonial enterprise. British settler colonies
L13@P0: had been established in many parts of the world, and the oldest of them had
L14@P0: fought and won a war for their independence.2 By the mid-nineteenth century, when Britain established two remote and, from her perspective, relatively inconsequential colonies along the northwestern flank of North
L15@P0: America,3
L16@P0:  there was this long experience to draw on – as well as the particular cast of British thought in the mid-nineteenth century. One element of
L17@P0: the latter was the drift towards free trade, which had culminated in 1846
L18@P0: and had forced a reconsideration of the relationship between colony and
L19@P0: mother country. Another was the legacy of a liberal humanitarian tradition
L20@P0: emphasizing the civilizing mission and the rights of Native peoples, which
L21@P0: had dominated the Colonial Office in the 1830s, and which had led to such
L22@P0: relatively generous arrangements with them as the Treaty of Waitangi, negotiated with the Maori in New Zealand in 1840. On the other hand, and
L23@P0: working against the humanitarian legacy, was a growing conviction, fed by
L24@P0: the growth of scientific racism before Darwin and by the evidence of uprisings against British authority (culminating in the Indian Mutiny of 1857-
L25@P0-1: 58), that Native peoples could not be assimilated and therefore had to be4 The Colonial Period
L26@P1: forcibly repressed in the interests of colonial security. Timing was important.
L27@P1: The founding of the colonies of Vancouver Island and British Columbia,
L28@P1: and the Native policies associated therewith, partook of both a long colonial
L29@P1: history and of a particular mid-nineteenth-century historical moment.
L30@P1: At the hub of the colonial system in 1850, as for fifty years before, was the
L31@P1: Colonial Office in London. Considering the size and geographical reach of
L32@P1: the British empire, the Colonial Office was a modest operation. It comprised two houses close to the prime minister’s residence on Downing Street,
L33@P1: which contained desks for most of the some thirty people who worked in
L34@P1: them, and a “library” which kept a few maps and books but was principally
L35@P1: a depository for official papers. For years the waiting room for visiting dignitaries and others with appointments was a tiny twelve-by-thirteen-foot space,
L36@P1: which could expand into standing room in a hallway. The secretary of state
L37@P1: for the colonies, who presided over this domain, held a cabinet position.
L38@P1: Under him was a permanent undersecretary, at least one other undersecretary,
L39@P1: and some twenty clerks. The most senior of the latter were, in effect, policy
L40@P1: advisors (some were considerable scholars), and the most junior were simply
L41@P1: copyists. Every communication from the Colonial Office was reproduced in
L42@P1: triplicate, and much incoming material was copied or précised, mostly still
L43@P1: by hand. There was a librarian, also for a time a geographer (responsible for
L44@P1: maps), and there were a couple of porters, a couple of house managers, and
L45@P1: messengers as required. That, in effect, was the Colonial Office, the nerve
L46@P1: centre of much of a global empire (India was handled by a different office).
L47@P1: Dispatches came in and, depending on their importance, were minuted,
L48@P1: précised, and variously circulated. Replies were drafted, commented on, finalized, and copied. An astonishing volume of correspondence – the reports, requests, and instruction on which the managing of an empire depended
L49@P1: – passed through this small office. In a given week each of the undersecretaries and senior clerks characteristically dealt with events in quite different
L50@P1: parts of the world. The whole system turned on the memories and judgments of a small group of exceedingly able men.4
L51@P1: They were, of course, men of their day who shared its implicit assumptions about the superiority of European civilization. They also operated within
L52@P1: more explicit guidelines and theories, one of which, as the accommodation
L53@P1: of the Colonial Office itself suggests, was frugality. The Crown would provide defence against external aggression, but internally colonies were to become fiscally independent as quickly as possible. Earl Grey, secretary of state
L54@P1: for the colonies in 1849 when the Crown granted the proprietary colony of
L55@P1: Vancouver Island to the Hudson’s Bay Company, had been a leading advocate of free trade, including the termination of preferential tariffs on colonial
L56@P1: goods, policies adopted in 1846. A few years later he reflected on the position of colonies in these early free trade years.5
L57@P1-2:  What, asked Grey, was theirThe Imperial Background 5
L58@P2: role when they were no longer thought of as suppliers of raw materials to the
L59@P2: mother country? National prestige and colonial responsibilities were the essence of his answer. He was impressed by the image value of colonies for a
L60@P2: great power. He also thought that Britain had acquired responsibilities to
L61@P2: British settlers who had chosen to relocate themselves within the empire and
L62@P2: deserved the benefits of British protection, and also to Natives who would
L63@P2: not be able to fend off these same settlers and deserved to be protected from
L64@P2: them. The honour of the Crown was at stake. He did not add, but might
L65@P2: have, that the coffers of the Lords of the Treasury opened reluctantly for honour. In an era of free trade, there was little political will to subsidize colonies,
L66@P2: and colonial governors around the world had to deal with such parsimony.
L67@P2: The Colonial Office also drew on a more formal body of theory, grounded
L68@P2: in the political economy of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, about the relationships of land, labour, and capital in colonial settings, and about their
L69@P2: bearing on colonial land policy. Such theory sought to manage social relations and hence to shape colonial societies in places where the prior balance
L70@P2: among the factors of production had been abruptly destabilized. By controlling land price and the rate of immigration, it was held, government
L71@P2: could establish the value of labour and, thereby, determine the nature of the
L72@P2: colonial social hierarchy. Edward Gibbon Wakefield, the most influential
L73@P2: exponent of such views, argued that the system could be calibrated so that
L74@P2: the colonial capitalist would have relatively cheap labour and the labourer
L75@P2: would become, in time, a property-owning freeholder. The mother country
L76@P2: would rid herself of surplus population, and all classes, constrained in Britain
L77@P2: by want of space, would improve their lot in colonies where land was neither
L78@P2: so cheap that almost anyone could have it nor so expensive that the poor
L79@P2: could never acquire it.6
L80@P2:  In this view, the colonies were, in effect, theatres for
L81@P2: an early form of social engineering, which, if the balance of land, labour, and
L82@P2: capital were got right, would retain the best and eliminate the worst forms
L83@P2: of British society. Such ideas raised basic questions. Marx, who considered
L84@P2: Wakefield the pre-eminent political economist of the 1830s (he had a low
L85@P2: opinion of political economists), gave him a good deal of critical attention:7
L86@P2: years later the American historian Frederick Jackson Turner offered a somewhat mystical American variant of Wakefieldian thought in his celebrated
L87@P2: article about the relationships between American society and the availability
L88@P2: of free land on the frontier.8 Wakefield’s theories, in short, were important.
L89@P2: They tended to break down in practice, partly because colonial officials could
L90@P2: rarely control access to land on distant frontiers, but he had put his finger on
L91@P2: a set of important relationships between society and land. Many in the midcentury Colonial Office were convinced Wakefieldians.
L92@P2:  More relevant to my purposes in this book were theories, also current in
L93@P2-3: the mid-nineteenth century, about what colonizers should do with the prior6 The Colonial Period
L94@P3: inhabitants of their colonies. Immigrants came to settle in colonies and colonial administrations had to make space for them. To do so they had to
L95@P3: dispossess indigenous people of much of their land and, in so doing, to
L96@P3: decide where to put and how to treat them. The problem occurred wherever Europeans established settler colonies, and by the mid-nineteenth century the Colonial Office had a good deal of experience to draw on. There
L97@P3: had been much discussion and a good deal of writing on the matter. Some of
L98@P3: the best of it was by Herman Merivale, who was the permanent undersecretary at the Colonial Office when the colonies of Vancouver Island and British Columbia were established, and previously had been the Drummond
L99@P3: Professor of Political Economy at Oxford. There in 1839, 1840, and 1841
L100@P3: he had delivered a set of lectures on colonization and colonies.9
L101@P3:  Two of
L102@P3: them were on what then was known as the “Native question,” and they are
L103@P3: as good a place as any to introduce the thought in the Colonial Office on the
L104@P3: matter and begin an analysis of it in British Columbia.
L105@P3: Merivale took European civilization, Native savagery, the superiority of
L106@P3: colonial power, and the sovereign rights of colonizers to colonial land completely for granted. Natives could resist but could not prevent what their
L107@P3: colonizers wished to do. The challenge, therefore, was to work out “the
L108@P3: duty and right policy of colonists and colonial governments towards the
L109@P3: Native inhabitants of the regions which they occupy.”10 He was under no
L110@P3: illusions about the European colonial record, full as he felt it was with
L111@P3: “wretched details of ferocity and treachery,” and about the limited value of
L112@P3: good intentions. Needed were practical measures that might lead to “small
L113@P3: successes.” All evils could not be corrected: the imperial centre was too far
L114@P3: from the “outcasts” and “degraded creatures” who marked the van of European colonial expansion. “Desolation,” wrote Merivale, “goes before us,
L115@P3: and civilization lags slowly and lamely behind.” At the same time he thought
L116@P3: that colonial officials themselves would no longer treat Native people “with
L117@P3: injustice and oppression,” and that they did have some means to improve
L118@P3: Native lives.
L119@P3: After a colony was established and Native violence was subdued, Merivale
L120@P3: thought that the protection of Natives from settlers was a prime duty of
L121@P3: colonial administrators. Innumerable “subjects of irritation” lay between the
L122@P3: two, for their interests were opposed, and colonial administrations had the
L123@P3: responsibility to protect the weaker party. There were two ways, he thought,
L124@P3: to accomplish this. One was to appoint officials – Merivale called them protectors or commissaries of the Indians – to act on behalf of Native people.
L125@P3: They would detect and prosecute offences against Natives, regulate contracts between them and whites, act as ex-officio defenders of Natives when
L126@P3: complaints or charges were brought against them, and control summary
L127@P3-4: corporal punishments of Natives by white employers or travellers. The otherThe Imperial Background 7
L128@P4: was to remove authority over Natives from colonial legislatures, which, invariably, would be controlled by settlers whose colonial opportunity depended
L129@P4: on the displacement of Natives. Rather, Merivale thought, authority over
L130@P4: Natives should lie with the central executive, that is, with the Colonial Office and the governor. He considered distance an advantage in this case,
L131@P4: allowing a dispassionate arbitration between competing interests.
L132@P4: Merivale considered such protection a short-term necessity rather than a
L133@P4: permanent solution. The civilizing mission, the need for which he took for
L134@P4: granted, was more important in the long run. Native people had to be transformed from a savage to a civilized state, and as he thought about this, their
L135@P4: “physical circumstances” – by which he meant where they should live – came
L136@P4: immediately to mind. An error of much earlier colonization, he thought,
L137@P4: was that land had not been allocated for Native use. As European settlement
L138@P4: proceeded, Natives were pushed off their former lands and hunting grounds,
L139@P4: and eventually the “dispirited, degraded ... remnants of once powerful tribes”
L140@P4: either threw themselves on the mercy of governments or loitered dangerously around the edge of European settlements. Only then had reserves
L141@P4: been allocated and attempts made to Christianize and civilize the disoriented survivors. Modern colonization, he thought, would not repeat these
L142@P4: errors. Reserves of land would be made at the beginning of colonization,
L143@P4: and the Natives would be somewhat “insulated” from settler society. Yet
L144@P4: Merivale doubted that even insulation on reserves – which he called the
L145@P4: missionary solution – could be more than temporary. In time, reserve lands
L146@P4: would be surrounded and coveted by settlers, and governments would capitulate to settler demands. The Natives would be relocated, and the cycle
L147@P4: would repeat itself. Agricultural progress and other advances towards civilization would be lost with each move back into the wilderness, while the
L148@P4: Natives, insecure and facing annihilation, would sink into “sullen apathy.”
L149@P4: Merivale had American experience in mind: in its light he considered reserves to be essential in the short run, but feared that in the longer term they
L150@P4: could entrap backward, demoralized peoples.
L151@P4: The only solution, he thought, was amalgamation, by which he seems to
L152@P4: have meant a form of acculturation between colonists and natives, including
L153@P4: miscegenation, that is not easily distinguished from assimilation.11 In his
L154@P4: view, Natives and colonists should live together as master and servant, as
L155@P4: fellow labourers, as husband and wife, and, ultimately, as fellow citizens. He
L156@P4: thought that all colonial Native policy should be directed to this end, and
L157@P4: that there was real urgency, otherwise Native races would perish. To those
L158@P4: who thought that Native people would inevitably fade away before the European coming, he replied that there was no supporting biological evidence.
L159@P4-5: Native numbers had declined since contact largely because of disease or warfare, not from “some unknowable other cause.”12 In some places Native8 The Colonial Period
L160@P5: populations were increasing. To those who thought that savage races could
L161@P5: never be civilized, Merivale replied that he did not know whether Natives
L162@P5: were the intellectual equal of Europeans, but was sure that they could benefit from civilization. He attached great importance to missionaries, and reported some of their achievements favourably while doubting that isolated
L163@P5: theocratic settlements were possible in the long run. Real amalgamation,
L164@P5: embracing not only conversion but also “the education of knowledge and
L165@P5: industry, and admission into the pale of civilized life,” had never been tried.
L166@P5: Until it had “the language of despair [was] unreasonable and unjust.” Amalgamation implied the spatial integration of settlers and Natives, the opposite
L167@P5: of a policy of insulation.
L168@P5: Like Wakefield, Merivale dealt with relationships between land and society in colonial settings, but shifted the emphasis from the cost to the location of land and, in so doing, emphasized crucial relationships between society
L169@P5: and space. The spatial arrangements that colonial governments would make
L170@P5: for Native people would matter enormously. Their lives would be very different if they were confined on reserves or interspersed within colonial society. Drastically different human geographies of Native life, with all their
L171@P5: ramifications, were at stake. Merivale, who held that Natives should be isolated in the short run and integrated in the long run, had two geographical
L172@P5: agendas, each of which was a potential land policy in a colonial setting. Each,
L173@P5: before long, would be vigorously advocated in British Columbia. Moreover,
L174@P5: his argument that control of such policies – and therefore of the human
L175@P5: geographies they entailed – should rest with the Colonial Office rather than
L176@P5: with colonial legislatures because the interests of settlers and Natives were
L177@P5: opposed, bears, even today, on federal-provincial divisions of power and on
L178@P5: arguments over referendums.
L179@P5: Merivale’s views about the atrocities of an earlier colonialism, the capacity
L180@P5: and willingness of Native peoples to acquire the benefits of civilization, and
L181@P5: the requirements of an enlightened colonialism to treat them honourably,
L182@P5: were not isolated opinions. Less than a decade before his lectures, parliament had abolished slavery throughout the British possessions, and in 1840,
L183@P5: while Merivale was still at Oxford, the Crown had guaranteed the Maori of
L184@P5: New Zealand possession of all their land, protection from European land
L185@P5: speculators, and equal rights and privileges with British subjects in the Treaty
L186@P5: of Waitangi. Such developments, like Merivale’s lectures, grew out of a broad
L187@P5: tradition of liberal humanitarianism that was rooted in the Enlightenment
L188@P5: and in early nineteenth-century Protestant evangelical Christianity. By the
L189@P5: 1830s it considerably influenced the Colonial Office and acquired a good
L190@P5: deal of parliamentary power.13 The liberal humanitarians assumed that all
L191@P5: people were essentially similar, and that with proper laws, administration,
L192@P5-6: and education, barbarians and savages could be civilized, a state they wouldThe Imperial Background 9
L193@P6: readily embrace when exposed to its advantages. They posited a universal
L194@P6: humanity and before long (with proper instruction) a universal, civilized
L195@P6: culture, a product of a common sociocultural evolution – allowing next to
L196@P6: no room for continuing cultural difference, and hardly a hint of the idea that
L197@P6: there were different forms of civilized human societies. Imbricated with the
L198@P6: moral crusade to Christianize and civilize was the economic agenda of free
L199@P6: trade. Monopolies of any kind were inefficient, free labour was more productive than slave labour, and a productive labour force would enlarge markets for British manufactures. The rights of property, an industrious labour
L200@P6: force given to hard work and thrift, a free market, an ordered Christian
L201@P6: society: this bourgeois vision set an agenda for the reform of the indolent
L202@P6: British poor and for the liberation and civilization of savage peoples overseas. The Aborigines Protection Society, the aim of which was the more
L203@P6: humane treatment of colonized peoples, emerged directly out of the struggle for the abolition of slavery, and counted among its leaders prominent
L204@P6: members of the Church Missionary Society and of the Liberal (free trade)
L205@P6: party. In short, the conflation of a moral vision and an economic agenda
L206@P6: gave the liberal humanitarians a good deal of momentum, and generated the
L207@P6: body of thought within which Merivale’s Oxford lectures and, for a time,
L208@P6: much of the thought in the Colonial Office about the “Native question”
L209@P6: was situated.
L210@P6: In the hands of officials in the Colonial Office, such views could yield
L211@P6: policies completely at variance with settler opinion in the colonies. In December 1835, the secretary of state for the colonies in London, Lord Glenelg,
L212@P6: declared illegal a British military advance, inspired by settlers, into Xhosa
L213@P6: (Bantu) territory during the Fourth Frontier War in South Africa. It had
L214@P6: resulted in the creation of a new colonial territory, Queen Adelaide Province. Glenelg held, however, that justice lay with the Xhosa who had been
L215@P6: provoked by innumerable settler aggressions and for whom no provisions
L216@P6: for land had been made. Queen Adelaide Province was to be abandoned, a
L217@P6: preposterous decision in the eyes of most white South Africans. “Is it just,”
L218@P6: wrote one, “that a few thousands of ruthless, worthless savages are to sit like
L219@P6: a nightmare upon a land that would support millions of civilized men happily?”14 The Great Trek of the Boers, launched at this time, was partly an
L220@P6: attempt to get away from such policies.15 There were similar disjunctions in
L221@P6: the south Pacific. In 1836 the Colonial Office refused to let the promoters
L222@P6: of the new colony of South Australia sail until they agreed to accept “Aboriginal Protectors” appointed by the Crown, and to acknowledge that Aboriginals had rights to the land that had to be purchased – policies that had
L223@P6: been unknown in Australia and that the promoters did their best to circumvent as soon as distance shielded them from the Colonial Office.16 Yet the
L224@P6-7: recognition that before colonization could proceed land should be acquired10 The Colonial Period
L225@P7: from Natives by treaty or purchase was a central objective of the liberal humanitarians, and it had surfaced again in New Zealand, to the dismay of

L227@P7: For all its fervour, the humanitarian discourse confronted the contradictions inherent in colonialism and was longer on good intentions than on
L228@P7: practical solutions. The full flood of reformist indignation and the thinness
L229@P7: of its practical solutions are both revealed in a report of a Select Committee
L230@P7: on Aboriginals that included some of the most influential reformers (Fowell
L231@P7: Buxton and William Gladstone among them) to the House of Commons in
L232@P7: June 1837.18 The committee was sure that British colonialism had been calamitous for the colonized: it had “incurred a vast load of crime.” Yet it was
L233@P7: the responsibility of the civilized, especially given their preponderance of
L234@P7: power, to promote the spread of civilization and to secure to Native people
L235@P7: “the due observation of justice and the protection of their Rights,” the most
L236@P7: important of which was their right to land. Europeans had arrived uninvited
L237@P7: in Native territory, and “by taking possession of their hunting grounds ... we
L238@P7: have despoiled them of their means of existence.” Yet the very colonies in
L239@P7: which Natives were to have “an incontrovertible right to their own soil,”
L240@P7: were also to provide an outlet for the “superabundant populations of Great
L241@P7: Britain and Ireland.” The committee’s attempts to protect Native rights and
L242@P7: also to provide for settlers – the moral dilemma at the core of settler colonialism – were sketchy and unconvincing: by vesting authority for Native people with the two houses of parliament and the Queen rather than with settlers,
L243@P7: by allowing only the Crown to purchase or acquire land from Native people,
L244@P7: and by discouraging local governments from making treaties because Native
L245@P7: people would understand neither the process nor its consequence and advantage would be taken of them. The report did not make clear how the
L246@P7: colonial government was to acquire land for the emigrating British and Irish
L247@P7: poor, or what to do should Native people not want to part with it. On such
L248@P7: matters the committee was silent, apparently assuming that beneficent administrators would negotiate scrupulous, transparent purchases, and that
L249@P7: Natives, eager for the benefits of civilization, would want to dispose of their
L250@P7: land.
L251@P7: In retrospect, Merivale gave his Oxford lectures when the influence of
L252@P7: liberal humanitarians was beginning to wane. Through the 1840s and 1850s
L253@P7: the movement’s contradictions, doubtful assumptions, and few practical solutions for the problem of protecting Native people within actively colonizing regimes became increasingly evident, and British colonial thought turned
L254@P7: away from a universalistic vision of a common humanity that had considered
L255@P7: savagery to be a convertible condition. Instead, colonialism slowly fell back
L256@P7: on more immutable, racially defined categories, on the economic rather than
L257@P7-8: the humanitarian side of the reform agenda, and on assumptions about forceThe Imperial Background 11
L258@P8: rather than education as the basis of colonial order. In the background were
L259@P8: new “scientific” ideas about race, including, in these years before Darwin,
L260@P8: the polygenist argument that human groups had different biological origins
L261@P8: (therefore, in the extreme view, different races were different species), phrenological findings about different skull sizes, and arguments that Africans were
L262@P8: the “link” between beasts and humans.19 As such ideas became current, a
L263@P8: vision of common humanity became harder to sustain. The colonial encounter itself seemed to furnish evidence. The colonized were not rushing to
L264@P8: embrace European civilization. Missionaries found it difficult to win converts, and many colonial frontiers were maintained by force of arms. Unrest
L265@P8: and falling sugar production in the West Indies complicated the claim that
L266@P8: free labour was an economic asset. The reform vision of a docile, industrious
L267@P8: labour force at the lowest ranks of an expanding British civilization did not
L268@P8: seem to describe what was happening to former slaves in the Caribbean, or
L269@P8: to Natives in New Zealand, South Africa, or India. Moreover, settlers pressed
L270@P8: for responsible government (in Canada Lord Durham’s report strongly recommended it), demands that ran counter to the reformers’ conviction that
L271@P8: responsibility for Aboriginals should stay in the Colonial Office. All of this
L272@P8: unsettled the humanitarian agenda. Its momentum seeped away in the 1840s,
L273@P8: and the Indian Mutiny in 1857-58 was close to a final straw.
L274@P8: In Australia and New Zealand, the two closest colonial antecedents of
L275@P8: British Columbia, the retreat from the spirit of humanitarian reform was
L276@P8: clearly evident by the 1840s. The Treaty of Waitangi had guaranteed “to the
L277@P8: Chiefs and Tribes of New Zealand ... the full, exclusive, and undisturbed
L278@P8: possession of their lands and estates, forests, fisheries, and other properties
L279@P8: which they may collectively or individually possess, so long as it is their wish
L280@P8: and desire to retain the same in their possession.”20 This left room to debate
L281@P8: the meaning of possession, and the New Zealand Company and its London
L282@P8: supporters held that the treaty guaranteed Maoris possession of no more
L283@P8: than their cultivated fields, villages, and burial sites. All other land was waste
L284@P8: and therefore Crown property. Moreover the Treaty of Waitangi, “made
L285@P8: with naked savages by a consul invested with no plenipotentiary powers,”
L286@P8: was not more than “a praiseworthy device for amusing and pacifying savages
L287@P8: for the moment” (similar arguments would be made about the Douglas
L288@P8: treaties on Vancouver Island). It was ridiculous that no more than 100,000
L289@P8: people, occupying perhaps 1 percent of the land, should hold up the British
L290@P8: colonization of New Zealand. Another parliamentary select committee, this
L291@P8: one convened in 1844 in response to New Zealand Company lobbying and
L292@P8: very different in tone from its predecessor eight years before, agreed (though
L293@P8: not unanimously). The Treaty of Waitangi was one of “a series of injudicious
L294@P8-9: proceedings.” Moreover, the right of Natives to all wild land in New Zealand, “was not essential to the true construction of the Treaty of Waitangi,12 The Colonial Period
